give your agent this skill asap, if you're a PM, issue trees are a key technique for breaking down a problem

use this when you already have a list of items (options, causes, segments, etc.) and you need to check if it is MECE

MECE means mutually exclusive (no two items overlap) and collectively exhaustive (no real case is missing). it does some magic behind the scenes to achieve this.

in addition, items in the same list must belong to the same ontology and represent correct parent-child relationships with the previous and next nodes.

01:44 SGTInvesting
One of the most expensive mistakes in the stock market is confusing high conviction with taking excessive risk.

Even the best companies can experience massive drawdowns.

Here’s why POSITION SIZING can make or break your portfolio.

You can identify a great company, have a strong investment thesis, and even get the technical setup right, but poor position sizing can still destroy your portfolio.

Here’s something every trader and investor should understand:
- 10% position falling 30% costs your portfolio 3%.
- 25% position falling 30% costs your portfolio 7.5%.
- 50% position falling 30% costs your portfolio 15%.

Same stock. Same decline. Completely different consequences.

A few lessons I’ve learned over the years:
- Never let conviction turn into overconfidence. Even your highest-conviction ideas can fail.
- Size positions based on risk, not excitement. Smaller, more volatile companies generally deserve smaller allocations.
- Protect your ability to stay in the game. A 50% portfolio drawdown requires a 100% gain just to recover.

Remember, the goal isn’t to make the most money from a single stock.

The goal is to compound your capital consistently over many years without allowing one mistake to wipe out years of hard work.

You don’t need to be right on every trade or investment to become successful.

But you absolutely need to survive the times when you’re wrong.

Position sizing is what keeps you in the game.

00:23 SGT quoteInvesting
I guess what I've seen from Chinese laser capacity expansion:

1. Dongshan/Source Photonics (索尔思): 9M/month capacity -> 22M/month Q4 -> 300m/year in 2027 (mostly EML, but blended)

Claims of 1B/year "target" for laser chips with no deadline, but I'd take this as a grain of salt.

2. Shijia (仕佳): 72M/year for 100mW CW, 2-3 year project (mainly 2029 full capacity online)

3. Yunling (云岭): 18.75M/year 70/100mW CW, 3 year schedule (mainly 2029 full capacity online)

4. Ligent (纳真), some reports stated 170M target for total capacity (also blended, lot of which is 200G EML)

5. Yuanjie: ~10M/year currently, expanding for early 2027 and 2028, but no quantities.

6. Hongchen: I think this was the perfect example of flooding H2 2026 arguments. With some some optical bears claiming 60-70M capacity...

But this turned out to completely wrong... Their actual statements were "70/100 mW products are entering small-volume production".

7. Dingxin Optoelectronics - Targeting 15M/year blended (with 70/100mW CW and 100G EML lines)

Obviously mapped many others like Everbright/Accelink and did some guesses around laser mixes, but only included public disclosures.

From your pluggable vendor channel checks:

- 70mW/100mW lasers are actually a bottleneck right now per Innolight/Cambridge channel checks, laser ASPs actually increasing.

Lasers are tighter than they were a few months ago.

I don't think there's a giant moat here, Chinese players are already competitive. But a bottleneck is a bottleneck, and anyone with capacity to monetize that will benefit, since it's a volume game.

In terms of what the larger pluggable makers are actually doing:

- Innolight September disclosure: actively introducing new suppliers and are planning to sign 2-3 year-long contracts to lock upstream capacity for lasers (still actively securing supply for 1.6T pluggables)

So there's some game theory over who can lock up qualified capacity among all your players.

Even if there's some over-ordering, laser BOM is cheap, so they'd probably want to lock up capacity with more suppliers than lose billions in downstream revenue. (also kinda hurts competitors)

- High end lines (for CPO), non-competitive with Western players like $LITE / $COHR as of next few years. But Chinese players would eventually develop the technology.

- $AAOI CEO: Chinese suppliers several years behind on high-power CPO/DWDM laser production "not in the next 2,3 years"

- $LITE CEO questioned whether claimed Chinese manufacturing capacity was translating into commercial output. "At least at the moment, we see no impact from any Chinese laser supply."

This is despite Shijia, Everbright, Yuanjie and others stating 400mW capabilities and capacity expansion targets from Chinese companies. Although Western CEOs might be disputing their reliability and capability to scale these lines.

I see lower end range bottleneck for pluggable will gradually ease as more capacity comes online 2028. But all evidence points against near-term overflooding.

The 100mW range for example, someone cited 2 years of equipment investment. Higher ranges were 3 years for equipment investment? So even some Chinese players take years for capacity to come online.

The multi year laser shortage statements from laser company executives seems to be true... especially among higher end ranges, since buildout takes a lot of time.

Legitimate competition coming from China, but as of now there's a scramble for CW LTAs among the industry in 2026-2027.

Lot of capacity is probably allocated toward higher spec lasers or EML, as seen with EML bottlenecking $LITE for the longest time (they have more supply now) that they had to buy CW off the market instead of supplying it themselves.

This is while tail end for 800G demand for example, might continue much much longer than expected with sovereign DC buildouts. So there might be some surprising dynamics for duration, we'll see.

In the end I do think supply chains will be bifurcated:

- Chinese players will prioritize domestic capabilities but heavily sources globally.

- Western players (now) prioritize Western supply chains unless China comes online with cheap enough supply (which don't see happening near-term).

TLDR:
-> Multi-year shortage definitely seems accurate for higher end specs
-> Lot of China capacity overflooding claims earlier from H1 turned out to be completely false. People keep making them for some reason across memory to photonics.
-> Chinese laser players are competitive for 70mW/100MW, meaningful expansion Y/Y, but nothing showing overflooding, given laser demand increasing, probably gradual easing into 2028.

We'll see, supply chain evolves month after month, just my current opinion from what I'm seeing.

agents are pretty good at a lot of stuff, but if you work on A/B tests, give them this to read:

- How Not To Run an A/B Test by Evan Miller: evanmiller.org/how-not-to-run…
- Evan Miller's sample size calculator: evanmiller.org/ab-testing/sam…
- Diagnosing Sample Ratio Mismatch, Microsoft's KDD 2019 paper: exp-platform.com/Documents/2019…
- Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi, Tang, Xu), companion site: experimentguide.com

start with evan miller’s article on peeking at experiment results.

if you check your test dashboard every day and stop the test the first time the result looks statistically significant, you greatly increase your false positive rate beyond the level that the p-value indicates.

19:05 SGT quoteInvesting
Yes, I like $SIVE. It's a fun company to cover, since there's a lot of supply chain alpha here.

But the company completely Tall Poppy Syndromed itself last earnings.

And it's clearly shown in the drawdown.

Bit of a longer consolidated thought and some scattered bits of supply chain info:

- Sivers has 100M CW DFB laser capacity coming online Q4 2027 during an industry shortage.

And very large allocations from foundries online (they were doing these quals with Win Semi + 2 others back in 2023/2024), so they can actively monetize the bottleneck today.

The other interesting reason why bottlenecks are important (aside from ASP hikes), is because qualifications convert much faster + more likely given incentives around supply scarcity.

-> As one example, module makers have expanded the amount of suppliers, eg. (lightcounting cited companies expanding to 5-7+ suppliers from 2-3).

Innolight, for example last month responded to a question addressing tight 1.6T DFB laser supply in 2026–2027:

- Innolight was actively introducing new suppliers last month and are planning to sign 2-3 year-long contracts to lock upstream capacity

-> This is while your biggest merchant laser companies making up the world's 600m+ EML/CW laser capacity like $COHR have redirected lasers to their own programs. $LITE sold out into 2029, Landmark also locked a lot of their capacity into 2027-2029. $AAOI was an expected player, but ended up redirecting lasers into their own transceiver programs too.

And this coincides with times $SIVE has tremendous capacity available now + actively engaged with Chinese pluggables players (not saying it's Innolight, but just shows Chinese makers like Cambridge/Eoptolink are actively trying to secure laser capacity).

- Fun to note, before $JBL was announced, Sivers had and has ongoing direct engagements with hyperscalers as well.

We saw that hyperscalers approached $MTSI and $AAOI for laser capacity from their earnings transcripts (and hilariously got turned away from AAOI due to shortages).

So the odds pluggable makers or hyperscalers end up converting to capacity agreements with $SIVE seems a materially higher.

Just a little rant: for all the sellside/retail trying to model revenue, you can't just slap on a stupid 25-35% CAGR on NRE revenue since it's close to 0 revenue now.

Especially when they scale up to maybe 300M laser capacity (extrapolated from 2:1 external/internal capacity).

It's also not the same as $POET having OE packaging capacity at scale, since lasers are in a genuine shortage. So capacity is more likely to convert like how $AAOI is sold out, $LITE is sold out into 2029

We've already seen what revenue that laser capacity brings in since $LITE cited $5B in laser capacity from just one 2028 fab alone in Greensboro (on higher end ranges).

And whatever lasers Sivers sell, they're targeting ~50-60+ blended gross margins long term on maybe $3-6 for lower range lasers to $6-$12 for high end custom deployments. But no disclosures around capacity -> revenue conversion yet from Sivers.

Now here's the thing people don't really understand, "why no revenue?" for current opportunities?

$SIVE pre 2024 focused on custom development for future architectural shifts like CPO.

For custom deployments:

- We finally got conversion from 1 of their 4 or so lidar customers this week with ~ $AEVA.
- ~ $APPL was confirmed ongoing earlier this year with an explanation that "It takes tremendous amount of trials and algorithms way beyond just what we supply to them".
- All their customers from 2023-2024 like Ayar and 3 others, probably achieve volume in 2028 as CPO takes off.

Custom high end lasers programs are extremely sticky but take many years and are mainly NRE. And as seen with CPO scale up, faced delays with commercialization over the years.

So $SIVE from the CEO shift in 2024 realized "okay" let's ramp revenue with mass commercialization products today like 70mW/100mW/200mW lasers for 800g/1.6T pluggables.

And that's where they found $JBL and all your other large pluggable players today during the shortage.

Now... the work Sivers did in 2023-2024 earlier: Such as $AAPL, Ayar, $AEVA, other lidar/CPO players.

And their new mass commercialization opportunities like $JBL, $GFS, and many pluggables/NPO suppliers in engagement now.

Have all their inflection points converges 2027 onward, which is why I find the company compelling.

Where I think management went completely wrong was messaging and near-term execution:

- Deciding to focus on current tiny contracts like Seminex, AllSpace, Tachyon orders felt like the entire focus recently in earnings, shareholder letters, and media commentary

-> Brutal honesty to $SIVE management, majority of Western audiences literally don't care and it's immaterial to the valuation.

$SIVE moved 0% on all of the Seminex/AllSpace/Tachyon order announcements, and even dropped in price. But rallied like 50% on $GFS and something similar on $JBL announcement.

The reason why most took long positions in the first place was CPO.

So if $SIVE wants to go answer questions to Swedish media about "Why are you bleeding out" and defending that with cellular orders explaining pipeline conversion.

That's not going to help people stay long during drawdowns.

-> Second part was not committing to NASDAQ listing in a certain timeframe and actually executing.

- If there's delays, sure, just say it, but non-committal lawyer-like language is infuriating to hear, especially from the CFO.

I think they'll have that opportunity next month earnings to correct everything.

So wrapping up:

- There's nothing I see remotely close to $SIVE, in terms of % of global CW laser capacity they're coming online with relative to MC.

- They have a ton commercialization paths, from O-Net, $POET, $JBL, Ayar, $GFS, $AAPL, $AEVA, and many potential hyperscaler/pluggable engagements.

Even if one or two fall through, the breadth of ongoing quals is so deep + current laser bottleneck is severe, that it's more likely than not many will convert to production.

It's clear $SIVE wants to focus on dominating the laser chokepoint first, and ended up using their 700m SEK fundraise for capacity expansion.

But they should focus on communicating the billions in potential economic scale from that laser capacity conversion.

And execute on it.

04:04 SGTInvesting
Why do Semiconductor stocks keep falling even though fundamentals remain strong?!

Here's why:

TLDR; The Semiconductor industry consumes a massive 20% of the total risk capital in the global equity markets.

The current share of risk capital for the Tech sector in the broader Global MSCI ACWI index is 40% vs. its 28% market cap weight. Of this, Semiconductors account for 20% vs. their 13% market cap weight.

Semis' market cap weight has risen rapidly in 2026 and because they're more volatile than the broader market, their share of risk runs well ahead of that weight. Therefore, investors are far more exposed to the Semis industry than even the index weights suggest.

This concentration then changes how the entire sector trades, where most of these selloffs are positioning events - not fundamental-driven.

Steady inflows into equities and thin net equity supply have kept realised vol low. Funds that size positions off VaR or vol-targeted risk budgets respond to low vol by running bigger gross exposure. When vol picks up, the same models force them to cut positions.

Then like a snowball rolling down a hill...that selling lifts vol further which forces the next round of cuts. (It works the opposite way too).

So with ~20% of the global risk budget sitting in Semis, these stocks are the first thing sold whenever risk models flag any shocks...even if fundamentals remain robust.

Data: JPM Global Markets Strategy

I believe $NAUT is worth several billion today, because it's on a path to enable us to cure deadly diseases like Alzheimer's with a single prompt by 2027-2028.

The breakthrough is not better protein measurement.

It is reading the state machine of human biology.

In Nautilus' tau paper, they found that phosphorylation is not random.

pT181 makes pT217 about 8x more likely to appear on the same intact tau molecule.

That matters because adding PO4 groups changes tau's charge distribution, which changes its conformation, which changes how tau binds microtubules.

Microtubules are the rails neurons use to move mitochondria, vesicles and proteins over enormous distances.

Tau helps stabilize those rails.

Change tau's molecular configuration enough and:

tau detaches → microtubules destabilize → transport breaks → neurons degenerate

Alzheimer's may therefore not be "too much phosphorylated tau."

It may be a progression through specific molecular states:

tau A → pT181 → pT217 → additional PTMs → pathological proteoform

And until now we largely could not read that combinatorial layer cleanly.

Mass spectrometry measures mass and charge extremely well, but two intact tau molecules can have the same mass while carrying the same phosphate at different positions.

Same atoms.
Same mass.
Very different biological behavior.

Fragmentation can help, but reconstructing the exact PTM configuration of millions of intact molecules becomes difficult.

Nautilus instead repeatedly interrogates the same intact protein with different probes.

Its tau assay currently reads isoform plus 7 phosphorylation sites, creating hundreds of potential molecular states, while reporting about 5.5% end to end CV versus about 25% cited by management as an industry benchmark.

And here is where this gets insane.

Biology does not appear to occupy every theoretically possible state.

Of 768 tau proteoforms their assay could resolve, they observed only 130 across all samples, and far fewer within individual biological systems.

That means the real state space may be highly constrained.

Now collect enough longitudinal data:

initial proteomic state + treatment → final proteomic state

Do that across millions of patients and interventions and AI stops being merely descriptive.

It becomes predictive.
Given molecular state X, what intervention moves the system toward healthy state Y?

That is effectively a biological key:lock search problem.

For tau alone, that could mean finding the intervention that prevents the proteoform trajectory that causes tau to abandon and damage the neuronal microtubule system.

But tau is just one vertical assay.

Add alpha synuclein.
Amyloid beta.
Cancer proteins.
Immune proteins.
Metabolic proteins.

Thousands more.

Eventually:

genome + proteoform state + treatment history → full body molecular state transition model

A genuine digital twin of human biology.

The endgame is not simply detecting disease earlier.
It is asking:

given this person's current molecular state, what intervention moves them back toward the healthy state?

And having an AI trained on billions of measured biological transitions produce the answer.

That is why I think $NAUT is building something much larger than a proteomics machine.

It is building the data layer required for AI to learn how to steer human biology.

Want to know how to avoid major drawdowns and improve your returns in the stock market?

Understanding Stan Weinstein's Stage Analysis is a great place to start. Every stock moves through 4 stages!

One of the most important lessons I've learned from Stan Weinstein's Stage Analysis is understanding where a stock stands in its market cycle and when to buy, hold, reduce exposure, or stay away.

The framework primarily uses the 30-week moving average (roughly equivalent to the 150-day SMA), price action, volume, and relative strength.

Stage 1: Basing / Accumulation

What does it look like?
- Usually forms after a prolonged Stage 4 downtrend
- Stock stops making consistent lower lows and starts trading sideways
- 30-week moving average begins to flatten
- Price moves above and below the flattening moving average
- Selling pressure decreases, and volume often dries up

What does it mean?
- The stock is trying to establish a bottom, but buyers haven't taken full control yet. This is where I start building my watchlist and looking for improving technicals, higher lows, and signs of accumulation.

- Remember, a stock falling 50-70% doesn't automatically make it a Stage 1 base. It needs time to stabilize and build a proper structure.

Stage 2: Advancing/Uptrend

What does it look like?
- Stock breaks out above its Stage 1 base
- Breakout ideally happens on expanding volume
- 30-week moving average starts sloping upward
- Higher highs and higher lows
- Relative strength improves against the broader market

What does it mean?
- Buyers are taking control, and institutional accumulation may be supporting the uptrend.

- This is my favorite stage to own growth stocks! I generally look for Stage 1 → Stage 2 breakouts and constructive pullbacks to rising moving averages.
- The goal isn't to buy at the absolute bottom but to participate when the stock starts showing evidence of a sustainable uptrend.

Stage 3 vs. Stage 4 - This is where a lot of us make mistakes!

Stage 3: Topping / Distribution

What does it look like?
- Usually forms after a prolonged Stage 2 advance
- Momentum slows, and price starts moving sideways
- 30-week moving average begins flattening
- Price repeatedly crosses above and below the moving average
- Breakouts start failing, and selling volume may increase
- Major support levels are still holding

What does it mean?
- The previous uptrend is losing momentum, and the stock may be going through distribution.

- Stage 3 doesn't automatically mean a crash is coming. Some stocks consolidate and resume their uptrends.

- For me, this is where I become cautious, tighten risk management, consider trimming positions, and avoid aggressively adding exposure.

Stage 4: Declining / Downtrend

What does it look like?
- Stock breaks below major support or its Stage 3 range
- 30-week moving average starts sloping downward
- Price trades below the declining moving average
- Lower highs and lower lows
- Short-term rallies often fail near declining moving averages

What does it mean?
- Sellers are in control, and the stock is in a downtrend.

- One of the biggest lessons I've learned is that technicals often reveal weakness before fundamentals do.

- A company can continue reporting strong earnings while its stock is entering Stage 4 because the market is already pricing in future expectations.

The biggest difference between Stage 3 and Stage 4:

Stage 3 = Sideways price action, flattening moving averages, potential distribution.
Stage 4 = Support breakdown, declining moving averages, established downtrend.

Another important thing to understand is that Stage 1 and Stage 3 can look very similar!

Both involve sideways price action and flattening moving averages. The difference is what happened before:

- Sideways consolidation after a prolonged decline could be Stage 1.
- Sideways consolidation after a major advance could be Stage 3.

My approach is simple:
Stage 1 - Build your watchlist and prepare.
Stage 2 - Look for opportunities to participate.
Stage 3 - Protect your gains and manage risk.
Stage 4 - Protect your capital and avoid weak downtrends.

Stage Analysis isn't perfect, but it's one of the most valuable frameworks I've learned in my investing and trading journey.

I use technicals to understand WHEN to participate and fundamentals to understand WHAT I'm buying.

Understanding these four stages can make a tremendous difference in how you navigate market cycles!

Superman @thesupermannx · 22 Oct 2026, 20:53 SGT
Scientists found a way to flush Alzheimer’s plaque out of the brain in minutes.

Without any surgery and drugs.

Your brain has a waste-clearance network called the glymphatic system. It flushes out toxic proteins and dead cells.

But it only really activates during deep, slow-wave sleep.

If you don't sleep, the trash piles up. Over time, that buildup leads to cognitive decline and Alzheimer's.

Until today.

Researchers just published a paper proving they can manually trigger this cleaning cycle.

Without you ever going to sleep.

They used 40.68 MHz ultrashort waves (USW) beamed non-invasively into the brain.

Within 10 minutes, the brain's fluid flow rapidly accelerated.

The waves artificially synchronized the neurons into a Delta state, the exact frequency of deep sleep. This forced the brain's water channels to open and start flushing out the system.

They tested it on mice with traumatic brain injuries and Alzheimer's pathology.

The brain swelling dropped. The toxic proteins were cleared out. Cognitive deficits actually improved.

No surgery. No massive chemical interventions. Just a frequency.

The US government cannot afford higher interest rates.

If interest rates average +150 basis points above CBO’s February projections by 2036, US deficits would increase by nearly $6 trillion over this period.

The deficit would then rise to 8.8% of GDP, the highest level since WWII, excluding 2008 and 2020.

This would also push the US public Debt-to-GDP ratio to a record 133%, up from ~100% currently.

If rates average +50 basis points above projections, deficits would increase by nearly $2 trillion, lifting the Debt-to-GDP ratio to 124% by 2036.

Just weeks ago, the 10Y Note yield traded at ~5.30%, or ~100 basis points above CBO’s average projected rate over the next 10 years.

The US government needs rate cuts.

Invest in years, don't use margin you can't cover, and stay updated so you only hold winners.

One interesting thing I've been noticing lately is that the market seems to be rewarding companies with strong free cash flow, healthy cash balances, manageable debt, and reasonable valuations, while punishing companies with high debt and weaker balance sheets.

During market corrections, financially stronger companies generally tend to hold up better.

Coming to semiconductors, I do expect some relief rallies as $SMH approaches its 200-day SMA around $500, which is a critical level to watch. But beneath the surface, a lot of technical damage has already been done.

Here's what I find interesting:

During the March 2026 correction, $QQQ was trading below its 200-day SMA, while semiconductors remained one of the strongest areas of the market.

Fast forward to October 2026, and the picture looks very different.

We're seeing failed breakouts, stocks losing their 200-day SMAs, and significant distribution across semiconductors.

Meanwhile, software has been showing impressive resilience and relative strength over the past few weeks and months, with several names forming Stage 1 bases or entering early Stage 2 uptrends.

There are still plenty of software names building bases, many of which I've shared over the past few weeks.

As for semiconductors, It's better to let the correction play out and wait for individual names to build proper Stage 1 bases before getting involved again.

A lot of technical damage has already been done, and it could take weeks or even months for some of these names to recover and rebuild their bases.

One important lesson from Stan Weinstein's Stage Analysis framework:

Don't wait for fundamentals to deteriorate before respecting a confirmed technical breakdown.

Price action often starts weakening long before the fundamentals reflect it.

Paradis@ParadisLabs
02:37 SGTInvesting
AI market colour:

TLDR; Two paths forwards:
1. If stocks keep falling - HFs still hold big positions on both sides so they'd have to dump their longs and buy back their shorts at the same time. Messy messy situation.
2. If stocks turnaround higher - HFs have a large amount of AI shorts on rn, so they'd have to buy those back = short squeeze territory.

So the current situation with AI stocks is that hedgies have pushed overall net exposure to the lowest level all year (latest GS PB data) with the L/S ratio for AI names near its lows.

Basically, that means there's a lot of room for them to get more long (cope, but true).

Across the entire book, HFs have mostly shorted against their longs rather than completely selling them, with short sales running at ~5x long buys in October MTD. That said, Tech has been hit from both sides with the record selling coming from long sales AND new shorts. FWIW, I don’t think there’s reason to panic since I highly doubt many funds out there are short the entire AI theme.

A lot of the longs are now concentrated in Mag 7 which is now a record ~22% of US net exposure. So in essence, the trade has been long stable megacaps, short the rest of the AI supply chain.

Funds don’t really have much room to add new long risk right now with gross already fairly elevated, so the way back for semis is by them covering shorts. A lot of the shorts recently have been put on in memory, photonics and the neoclouds, as well as Asian semis, so upside headroom is probably most significant in those areas.

Time will tell. Would not try to time bottoms here.

00:27 SGT quoteTech
Use /requirements-reconcile before you read long AI PRDs

If you get a long AI-written PRD or business requirements document, do not start by reading every page.

In long AI documents, requirements often contradict each other. For example, one page says users can delete records. Another page says records are never deleted. Both pages read well on their own, but they cannot both be true.

To deal with this, run /requirements-reconcile before you review anything long.

It will:

- scan the document
- find contradictions and overlaps
- give you one clear list of requirements that are in, out, or changed

Send that list back instead of 90 pages of comments.
